title: Kubernetes RBAC: Locking Down the Cluster with Least Privilege
summary: A dense handwritten-notes handbook on Kubernetes authorization: Roles, ClusterRoles, Bindings, ServiceAccounts, security contexts, and how to design least-privilege access that actually holds up in production.

chapters.title: RBAC Fundamentals & The Request Pipeline
points: RBAC = Role-Based Access Control: the Authorization step of every API request (Authn → Authz → Admission) — k8s checks verbs, not users' identities
Every RBAC decision answers: can SUBJECT (user/group/ServiceAccount) perform VERB (get/list/create/delete...) on RESOURCE (pods, secrets...) in NAMESPACE (or cluster-wide)
RBAC is purely additive (default-allow nothing): there is no deny rule — access exists only if some binding grants it
Built-in roles to know: cluster-admin, admin, edit, view — view can't see Secrets by design; edit can (huge escalation risk)
Users/groups are NOT API objects — they come from external auth (certs, OIDC, LDAP); ServiceAccounts ARE cluster objects you create
Discovery endpoints (/api, /apis, healthz) are world-readable and not RBAC-controlled — enumerating resources is always possible

chapters.title: Roles: Namespace-Scoped Permissions
points: Role object: rules[] of apiGroups, resources, verbs, scoped to the Role's own namespace (metadata.namespace matters)
verbs cheat-sheet: get, list, watch (read); create, update, patch, delete, deletecollection (write); impersonate, bind, escalate (dangerous)
get on a collection ≠ list: 'get pods' alone can't enumerate, only fetch by known name — combine deliberately
Subresources use slash syntax: pods/log, pods/exec, pods/portforward, secrets — pods/exec is effectively 'shell on any pod'
resourceNames: restrict rules to named objects, e.g. only 'get' the configmap 'app-config' — the least-privilege lever most people forget
wildcards: apiGroups: ['*'], resources: ['*'], verbs: ['*'] = admin everything in scope — audit for them in review

chapters.title: ClusterRoles: Cluster-Wide Power & Reuse
points: ClusterRole: same rules schema, no namespace — grants apply cluster-wide across all namespaces
ClusterRole is reusable via aggregationLabel/aggregationRule: managed ClusterRoles auto-union rules from matching labels (how k8s extends 'view'/'edit')
The namespace-flattening trick: a ClusterRole bound with a RoleBinding grants its permissions only in that one namespace — the standard pattern for reusable role templates
Non-resource URLs: ClusterRoles can cover /healthz, /metrics, /version via nonResourceURLs — needed for scraping Prometheus
ClusterRole can also govern cluster-scoped resources: nodes, namespaces, PVs, storageclasses, customresourcedefinitions
Deleting a ClusterRole breaks all Bindings referencing it silently — permissions vanish without an error on the binding itself

chapters.title: Bindings: RoleBinding vs ClusterRoleBinding
points: Binding = grants; Role never grants anything alone. RoleBinding lives in one namespace; ClusterRoleBinding spans the cluster
subjects: kind User, Group, or ServiceAccount — namespace field required for namespaced SAs (default: <ns>:default)
Matrix: Role+RoleBinding = one ns; ClusterRole+RoleBinding = one ns (reusable template); ClusterRole+ClusterRoleBinding = everywhere
Bindings are immutable in place: change a subject and the API rejects it — delete & recreate (brief permission gap; script it atomically)
auto-mount of 'system:' groups: system:masters = god mode; authenticated = every human user — never grant these casually
Binding references don't validate at creation with full strictness — typo'd subject kind or SA namespace fails open (grants nothing) or wrong (grants to nobody)

chapters.title: ServiceAccounts: Identity for Workloads
points: ServiceAccount = API identity for pods; tokens prove it; defaults: namespace's 'default' SA with almost no permissions
Legacy projected token auto-mount: every pod got its SA token volume at /var/run/secrets/.../token — a stolen pod = stolen credentials
Modern fix: automountServiceAccountToken: false (pod and/or SA level), or Kubernetes ≥1.24 bound tokens (short-lived, audience-bound, expiring JWTs)
One SA per workload, not shared 'default': blast-radius isolation — compromise of one app doesn't inherit another's permissions
create SA + token: kubectl create sa app-sa; kubectl create token app-sa (short-lived) vs secret-based long-lived tokens (avoid)
Workload Identity patterns: EKS IRSA / GKE Workload Identity map SA → cloud IAM so pods touch AWS/GCP without static keys

chapters.title: Security Contexts: Hardening the Pod Itself
points: securityContext at pod and container level: runAsNonRoot: true + runAsUser: 1000 — reject root images at admission
fsGroup & supplementalGroups: fix volume file permissions for non-root containers (emptyDir, PVCs)
readOnlyRootFilesystem: true + emptyDir for /tmp — blocks malware persistence via writable container fs
allowPrivilegeEscalation: false and privileged: false; cap drop ALL then add back only NET_BIND_SERVICE etc. (capabilities ~fine-grained root)
seccompProfile: RuntimeDefault (now default since 1.24 via the Restricted profile); seLinuxOptions for MAC enforcement
Pod Security Admission replaces PSP: labels on namespace (pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce=restricted) — 'restricted' profile ≈ all the above flags

chapters.title: Least-Privilege Patterns in Practice
points: Pattern: start with zero RBAC, watch the audit log for 403s (kubectl get events / apiserver audit), grant only the denied verbs — evidence-driven policy
Pattern: per-app namespace + per-app SA + one curated Role bound via RoleBinding to a shared ClusterRole template — consistent, auditable
Pattern: controller/operators need a ClusterRole but should filter by ownerReferences/labels in code, never wildcard-watch everything
Pattern: separate SAs per Deployment even in the same app (web vs migration job) so CI jobs can't touch runtime secrets
escalate/bind verbs: letting a user 'create RoleBindings' freely = privilege escalation — they can bind cluster-admin to themselves
Secrets are the crown jewels: read access to a Secret in a namespace ≈ full SA tokens there — Gatekeeper/OPA policies should restrict who can read secrets at all

chapters.title: Common Mistakes & Gotchas
points: Mistake: ClusterRoleBinding 'just to make it work' — one forgotten CRB on 'edit' exposes every namespace forever
Mistake: verbs on collections don't imply subresources — 'get pods' does NOT grant 'get pods/log'; list each subresource explicitly
Mistake: RBAC is enforced at the API server only — kubelet exec, port-forward via API, and anything bypassing apiserver skip these checks
Gotcha: list/watch on Secrets bypasses encryption-at-rest in etcd reads and dumps tokens — even 'view' role escalation via any Secret-bearing SA
Gotcha: impersonate verb + 'system:' groups = instant cluster-admin; guard impersonate like root
Debug flow: kubectl auth can-i --list --as=system:serviceaccount:ns:sa — the ground truth of what an identity can do; kubectl auth whoami
Rancher/Auth Webhook note: external authorizers (OPA, webhooks) run in addition to RBAC — deny there doesn't remove RBAC grants

chapters.title: Comparisons & Trade-offs
points: RBAC vs ABAC: ABAC (attributes) was removed as practical option — RBAC's coarse roles are auditable; fine-grained needs OPA/Gatekeeper/Kyverno on top
RBAC vs Node authorizer vs Webhook: kubelet uses Node authorizer; custom Webhook authorizers chain after RBAC — order: RBAC → Node → Webhook
ClusterRole vs duplicated Roles: CRs centralize but any mistake scales cluster-wide — trade consistency for blast radius
Narrow verbs+resourceNames vs broad roles: precise rules = review overhead & drift; broad roles = faster shipping, bigger compromise surface
Auto-mounted tokens vs no automount + IRSA: convenience vs credential-theft blast radius
Policy-as-code tools: rbac-manager, korb, kube-apiserver audit + rbac-lookup / krew auth — pick audit tooling before you have 50 roles

chapters.title: Summary: Your RBAC Checklist
points: Mental model: identity (SA/user) → binding → role → rules of verb+resource(+subresource+name) — read any grant in that order
Always: one SA per workload, automount off unless needed, runAsNonRoot + drop ALL caps + readOnlyRootFilesystem
Always: namespace scoping by default; ClusterRoleBindings only for platform components (controllers, CI runners) with a named owner
Never: bind edit/cluster-admin to groups of humans casually; grant secrets list cluster-wide; use system:masters for anything routine
Verify: kubectl auth can-i --list --as=…, apiserver audit logs for 403s, periodic rbac-lookup scan for wildcard rules and orphaned bindings
Evolve: start zero → audit-driven grants → codify in Git (RBAC as code + PR review) → enforce with PSA restricted + policy engine
Remember: RBAC is additive, API-server-only, and Secrets are credentials — design assuming any pod's token will eventually be stolen
